content: Trauma is one of the leading causes of death and disability, particularly among young individuals. Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a significant contributor to mortality in this population. Trauma patients are at an elevated risk of developing deep vein thrombosis (DVT), with the incidence varying depending on the diagnostic method and the location of the thrombosis. This increased risk is primarily due to prolonged immobility and coagulation abnormalities following trauma. Thromboprophylaxis, which can be mechanical (e.g., compression devices) or pharmacological (e.g., anticoagulants), has the potential to reduce both mortality and morbidity in trauma patients who survive beyond the first day of hospitalization by lowering the risk of VTE. However, a systematic review conducted over a decade ago did not find conclusive evidence supporting the effectiveness of either mechanical or pharmacological thromboprophylaxis. This review, however, was based on studies of generally poor quality. Since then, new trials have been conducted, and current clinical guidelines recommend the use of thromboprophylaxis in trauma patients. Despite this, there has not been a comprehensive and updated systematic review since the earlier one. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of thromboprophylaxis on mortality, as well as the incidence of DVT and pulmonary embolism (PE), in trauma patients. Additionally, the study aimed to compare the effectiveness of different thromboprophylaxis methods and assess their impact based on the type of trauma. To gather relevant data, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Injuries Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PubMed, and others, up to April 2009. The inclusion criteria for the study were randomized controlled trials involving individuals of any age with major trauma, defined by physiological instability (e.g., penetrating or blunt trauma affecting more than two organs with unstable vital signs), anatomical severity (Injury Severity Score >9), or high-energy mechanisms of injury. Trials focusing solely on outpatients, hip fractures, or acute spinal injuries were excluded. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by four authors working in pairs, with disagreements resolved by a fifth author. A total of 16 studies involving 3,005 participants were included in the analysis. Four trials compared the use of any type of thromboprophylaxis (mechanical and/or pharmacological) versus no prophylaxis. The results demonstrated that thromboprophylaxis significantly reduced the risk of DVT in trauma patients (relative risk [RR] 0.52; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.32 to 0.84). Mechanical prophylaxis alone was shown to reduce the risk of DVT (RR 0.43; 95% CI 0.25 to 0.73). Pharmacological prophylaxis, however, was found to be more effective than mechanical methods in reducing DVT risk (RR 0.48; 95% CI 0.25 to 0.95). Among pharmacological options, low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) appeared to be more effective than unfractionated heparin (UH) in reducing DVT risk (RR 0.68; 95% CI 0.50 to 0.94). Furthermore, the combination of mechanical and pharmacological prophylaxis was associated with the lowest risk of DVT (RR 0.34; 95% CI 0.19 to 0.60). The authors concluded that there was no evidence to suggest that thromboprophylaxis reduces mortality or the incidence of PE in trauma patients. However, there was evidence, albeit of moderate strength, that thromboprophylaxis prevents DVT. Based on these findings and extrapolating from evidence in related conditions such as surgery, the authors recommend the use of any DVT prophylactic method for patients with severe trauma.
